Today and tomorrow, we’ll explore what could happen if each party overperforms expectations in the November midterm elections. Tomorrow, we’ll look at what could happen if Democrats sweep the House and Senate. 

   Today, let’s examine what might happen if the GOP has a big Nov. 3 victory:

   • President Trump would be able to spend the final two years of his presidency keeping GOP control of Congress, which would be an enormous tailwind for his domestic and foreign policies. Some version of the $5,000 “Trump Dividend” that he promised would likely be paid. Congressional checks on White House power would remain diminished, and Trump would remain the most powerful figure in American politics—and beyond—heading into the 2028 presidential election.

   • 2028 would run through Trump. If he defied the odds and secured GOP control of Congress, his grip on the party would be tighter than ever, and the prospect of a successful GOP presidential candidate running without Trump’s endorsement would be very hard to imagine. JD Vance? Marco Rubio? Ted Cruz? It would all run through Trump. The influence of people like Tucker Carlson, who have turned on Trump, would likely diminish.

   • Democrats would be in total disarray. The party’s problems that were exposed in the 2024 presidential election but never truly addressed would be seen by some as so acute that it could raise a question of whether the Democratic Party of Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and Nancy Pelosi even exists anymore. There would be calls for the party to completely dismantle its existing structure and start over. In terms of governing, they might become completely irrelevant for Trump’s final two years.

   • Corporations that want regulatory relief, tariff changes or new policies would need to work with the White House. There would be no way around it. Congress would likely remain deferential on big policies like trade and immigration, and decisions about artificial intelligence would be led by the Trump administration.

   • Legacy projects for Trump would go into overdrive. The Kennedy Center, Triumphal Arch and White House ballroom projects would likely be joined by other initiatives. Also, Trump’s foreign-policy approach would likely continue. If voters signal an acceptance of his approach to the Middle East and Venezuela, it could give the GOP cover to support a broadening of this type of foreign policy in places like Cuba.

   Trump’s Monday: The president is scheduled to take part in three policy meetings today. Later, he is expected to make an announcement at 2 p.m. ET.

As case loads grow at Arkana Labs, they’re using Claude to help process referral paperwork with 97–98% accuracy, so patients still get results the day after a biopsy.   Learn More  >       What I’m Following     ASHLEIGH COLEMAN FOR WSJ   Democrats pour money into long-shot Mississippi Senate bid: In a sign of just how bullish some Democrats are feeling, some party officials and donors are starting to size up the potential of once-unthinkable seats in the Deep South. Inspired by success in places like Georgia, they see Scott Colom’s bid as a down payment for future victory in a state with a large Black population.

   How Trump’s economic agenda backfired on him. The White House theory on the economy rested on fiscal restraint that never arrived and overlooked how much of Trump’s agenda would feed the price pressures now pushing rates higher. Tariffs raised the cost of imported goods. The war with Iran sent oil and diesel prices soaring. Immigration restrictions shrank the labor force.

   Anthropic CEO dines with Trump at the White House. While Trump has championed U.S. progress in building advanced AI, his administration has been critical of Anthropic and its push to increase oversight of AI models. Sunday’s meeting between Trump and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei comes weeks after Amodei called for leading U.S. AI companies to slow down the pace of development. The gathering could represent an opportunity for the startup to improve its relationship with the administration.

       What Else Is Happening   • Defense contractors are spending billions to build factories and increase production to stock America’s nearly bare cupboard of highly engineered missiles. But those efforts haven’t translated into real gains yet.

   • British investigators are probing whether Iran or an Islamist group was behind a foiled attack on an air base in England that houses U.S. forces.

   • A Trump administration initiative to create a China-free supply chain for military and industrial inputs is starting to work.

   • Trump’s trade war and the Iran conflict have ignited Canada’s ambition to diversify its energy exports.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

U.S.-Iran conflict: Negotiators are pressing Iran to make a concession on its nuclear program to revive ceasefire talks with the U.S. after Trump rejected Tehran’s truce proposal.

 

Trump’s Monday: The president is scheduled to take part in three policy meetings today. Later, he is expected to make an announcement at 2 p.m. ET.

What I’m Following

Democrats pour money into long-shot Mississippi Senate bid: In a sign of just how bullish some Democrats are feeling, some party officials and donors are starting to size up the potential of once-unthinkable seats in the Deep South. Inspired by success in places like Georgia, they see Scott Colom’s bid as a down payment for future victory in a state with a large Black population.
